items.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I was in the last part of the band, where it was Ron Carter, George Coleman, Harold Mabern, and an alto player.

ctx.x: Stitt was there, yeah. Stitt took Trane’s place, but after Stitt it wasn’t any – I don’t remember anybody else being there. It was Sonny. Miles wanted him in there to play alto, but Sonny was traveling with alto and tenor. He wants to play them both all the time. But when he played the alto, people went crazy. They’d say, “Yeah!,” because he was reminiscent of Charlie Parker. But he wanted to play – on the gig, he wanted to play the tenor too, and Miles didn’t want him to play the tenor. So Miles used to tell…

been through that with everybody was in the band before. So he said, “No, we can’t use him.” [Harold] Lovett, Miles’s lawyer and friend, suggested that he get Tony Williams, who at the time I think was working with Jackie McLean. So he got Tony in the band. Tony was so young, he couldn’t – at that time, he probably couldn’t get into these clubs without Miles bringing him there. So he got Tony. Then they had Wayne Shorter and that band that they had. I was in the last part of the band, where it was Ron Carter,…

items.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: And Ron Carter was going to be in the band, and Jimmy Cobb was just finishing up a tour so Tony Williams was going to join the band. And we had a great six weeks.

ctx.x: In ’63, before Herbie Hancock. Only a few people know about that. April 1963. And we had a great time too. See here again, Miles used to be from Chicago with them, ‘cause I’ve never pursued a gig, see I never called up a guy and said, “Hey man, give me a gig,” because that’s never been my thing, even before I could put two notes together I always said that if you could play, if you’ve got, somebody will hear. So when I went out of town I was out with Roy Haynes’ quartet. Roy Haynes, Larry Wood Ridley, Frank…

got at Birdland. So somebody called and said, “You ain’t got no two weeks.” So I got up and my wife said, “Oh by the way call Betty Carter, she’s got two weeks for you at Birdland.” I was just, it was maybe five years, I don’t know. So she said also, “Do you know somebody named Prophet?” Well Prophet, his name was Richard Jennings, he was a well talented artist, he could draw pictures and paintings with birds, and Miles loved him and everybody knew him. And he knew I could comp. And Joe Griffin knew I could comp.…

And to this day I still do that because see I always tell people — somebody asked me a question and I said well you know I consider myself a blues piano player that understands the philosophy of jazz. So I told Fred and he said, “You said that?” He said, “I like that.” That’s what I am. I’m going to always be, because blues or jazz comes from the blues.
